findings.claim: The Nicene Creed opens with the declaration “We believe in one God” before naming the three persons in turn.
findings.truth: The creed recited at Mass in English since 2011 is in the first person singular: “I believe in one God”. “We believe” is the withdrawn 1973 translation. The same lesson quotes the opening correctly two paragraphs later (“I believe in one God, the Father almighty…”), so the lesson contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Roman Missal: the 2011 ICEL translation opens “I believe in one God, the Father almighty”; internal inconsistency with narration block n11

findings.claim: The creed is quoted three times in the lesson (and once in the 6-mark model answer) as saying the Son is “of one substance with the Father”, including in the verbatim run “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father.”
findings.truth: The current English translation reads “consubstantial with the Father”. “Of one substance with the Father” is not the text Catholics recite; “of one Being with the Father” was the previous translation. ‘Consubstantial’ is the distinctive term a student is expected to reproduce.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Roman Missal: the 2011 translation renders consubstantialem Patri as “consubstantial with the Father”, replacing “of one Being with the Father”

findings.claim: The technical phrase “one substance, three persons” (homoousios) comes from the Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and is the basis of the Nicene Creed recited at every Mass.
findings.truth: Two errors in one sentence. Homoousios does not mean “one substance, three persons”; it means ‘of the same substance’ and describes the Son in relation to the Father. And the formula ‘one substance, three persons’ (una substantia, tres personae) is the Latin phrasing of the early Western Church, not a phrase from Nicaea. Nicaea defined the Son as homoousios with the Father; the Spirit was addressed at Constantinople in 381.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3.1 (‘as expressed in the Nicene Creed; the scriptural origins of this belief and its development in the Council of Nicaea’); the lesson’s own body text attributes ‘una substantia, tres personae’ to ‘the language of the early Church’, not to Nicaea

findings.claim: Every lesson ends with a practice question typed “2 marks — State / Give” (lessons 1, 2, 3 and 4).
findings.truth: This paper sets no 2-mark question. Each religion is examined by two five-part questions of 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks. A 2-mark item trains a question form the student will never meet; the natural home for a two-point answer is the 4-mark explain (2 marks per point). All four questions retiered to 4 marks, with the stem asking for a brief development of each point.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 assessment section (lines 244-275) and 4.4.1 (lines 1822-1834): ‘marks will be allocated as follows: 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12’

findings.claim: “The exam mark scheme rewards students who explain that they are complementary theological accounts” (exam tip) and “This is a mark-scheme-distinguishing answer” (content, imago Dei misconception box).
findings.truth: Both assert the contents of a board mark scheme that is not quoted or cited, and neither can be sourced. House rule: correct facts about format, describe answer quality in our own vocabulary, never claim what a mark scheme rewards.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md copyright-distancing rule; no mark-scheme source available

findings.claim: The Nicene Creed … “For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven: by the power of the Holy Spirit he became incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and was made man.” Presented as the creed’s “definitive formula”, and echoed in the conclusion, the exam tip and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The current text reads “For us men and for our salvation he came down from heaven, and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man.” The lesson’s version mixes the withdrawn 1973 wording with the new. The 6-mark model answer also quotes the creed as “on the third day he rose again”; the current text is “and rose again on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures”.
findings.evidence: 2011 ICEL translation of the Nicene Creed (Roman Missal); corroborated by Wikipedia, Roman Missal, on the 1973-to-2011 revision

findings.claim: The Nicene Creed declares: “We look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come.” Repeated in the 12-mark model answer as “we look for the resurrection of the dead”.
findings.truth: The current text reads “and I look forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.” The whole creed moved to the first person singular in 2011, so “We look for” is doubly out of date.
findings.evidence: 2011 ICEL translation of the Nicene Creed; Wikipedia, Roman Missal, confirms the first-person-singular opening “I believe in one God” in the same text

findings.claim: The Catechism summarises: each person receives a retribution of their souls in the particular judgement immediately after death.
findings.truth: The Catechism says each person receives their eternal retribution in their immortal soul at the very moment of death, in a particular judgement. “A retribution of their souls” garbles the teaching and reads as though the soul itself is what is handed out.
findings.evidence: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1021-1022 (particular judgement)

findings.claim: Eastern Orthodox Christianity … uses different terminology, speaking of “the toll houses” rather than purgatory.
findings.truth: The aerial toll houses are a disputed devotional teaching held by some Orthodox writers and rejected by others. They are not the Orthodox term for purgatory. The settled Orthodox position is that the Church prays for the dead but does not accept the Latin doctrine of purgatory; the process is described as deification (theosis), not legal purification.
findings.evidence: settled contrast between Latin and Orthodox teaching on the state of the dead; the toll-house teaching has no conciliar standing

findings.claim: Three lessons set a 4-mark question in the form “Explain two contrasting Christian beliefs about …” (creation, the death of Jesus, life after death).
findings.truth: The ‘contrasting beliefs’ rubric, with its instruction to refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one other tradition, belongs to the thematic studies paper, not the study-of-religions paper. On the religions paper the 4-mark item is normally ‘explain two …’ about the religion being studied. However the spec for this religion does require common and divergent views within Christianity, so contrasting Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant beliefs is legitimate examinable content. Options: keep as is; or restem to “Explain two different Christian beliefs about …” to avoid training the thematic rubric.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3 (‘Common and divergent views within Christianity … should be included throughout’) vs the thematic-studies rubric
findings.ruling: Leave: examinable content / spec names Nicaea.

findings.claim: 1-mark question and knowledge check both treat the Council of Nicaea (325 CE) as the council at which “the Trinitarian doctrine” was formally defined.
findings.truth: Strictly, Nicaea defined the Son as consubstantial with the Father; the Holy Spirit was addressed at Constantinople in 381, which is where the creed reached its Trinitarian form. The lesson body says this correctly. The spec names only Nicaea, so Nicaea is the answer the board expects. Options: leave both as they are; or widen the accepted answer to note Constantinople 381 completed the definition.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3.1 (‘its development in the Council of Nicaea’); the lesson’s own collapsible on Constantinople 381
findings.ruling: Leave: examinable content / spec names Nicaea.

findings.claim: The F6 edits restore the creed’s official wording “For us men and for our salvation”.
findings.truth: That is the exact 2011 liturgical text, so it is correct. Recording it because the gendered wording may read oddly in a school resource; the alternative is to paraphrase rather than quote. No further edit made.
findings.evidence: 2011 ICEL translation of the Nicene Creed

findings.claim: All four lesson descriptions run over 100 characters (104, 107, 111, 112).
findings.truth: Over the house validator limit, but the descriptions are accurate and nothing is wrong in them. Not edited.

summary: Doctrine, dates, councils, scripture references and all twenty knowledge-check answer keys are sound; the damage is concentrated in the Nicene Creed, which is quoted throughout in the withdrawn 1973 translation ("We believe in one God", "of one substance with the Father", "We look for the resurrection of the dead") rather than the text Catholics actually recite, plus a wrong attribution of "one substance, three persons" to Nicaea. Every lesson also ends with a 2-mark practice question, a form this paper does not set.
